title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 2)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: The talk's main teaching is that our true nature is not something we can grasp or conceptualize, but rather it is beyond all dualities and limitations. By cultivating awareness and seeing things as they truly are, we can let go of our preconceptions and distinctions, revealing a deeper understanding of reality that is empty yet full, interconnected yet independent. This understanding allows us to see the world with fresh eyes, unencumbered by our conditioned perceptions, and connect with the ultimate reality that lies beyond all conceptual thinking.

I mean, I'm sorry, part two.
And it's called The Nature of Visual Awareness.
And there are several chapters in this one as well.
And I've really condensed these a lot more than I did last week, so hopefully they're not as long to get through.
So in part one, the nature and location of mind, after much deliberation, the Buddha establishes the existence of the true mind.
The Buddha now sets up arguments for recognizing the simple fact that we are aware.
And again, this awareness is ever-present and it's not reliant or dependent on objects.
This is a real strong point as we go through this section: ever-present and not reliant or dependent on objects.
In this section, he often, in conversation with others in the assembly, illustrates his points on this.
And although things move in and out of awareness, the awareness itself doesn't move.
The Buddha uses visual awareness to make this point.
And in fact, awareness is present in the same way with all of our sensory faculties.
So he's talking about the visual faculty right now.
But in fact, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and also thoughts in our mind really are in the same way related to this deeper awareness that doesn't move.
So the Buddha states at the end of the first chapter that the eyes simply reveal visible objects, but it is the mind that sees and not the eyes.
Chapter two in this section is called visual awareness does not move.
The Buddha then states that multitudes do not become arhats, which are totally awakened beings, because they're confused by afflictions that are like visitors and dust.
I like this next little section.
He then asks an arhat what caused him and five others to awaken and become sages.
And Ajna Taka Undiniya states:
*Because I have come to realize that visitor and dust signify what they signify, World Honored One, suppose a visitor stops at an inn for a night or for a meal.
Once his stay has ended or the meal is finished, he packs up his bags and goes on his way.
He's not at leisure to remain.
But if he were the innkeeper, he would not leave.
By considering this example of the visitor, the one who comes and goes, and the innkeeper, the one who remains, I understand what the visitor signifies.
He represents transients.
Again, suppose the morning skies have cleared after a rain, then a beam of pure light from the rising sun may shine through a crack in the door to reveal some motes of dust obscuring the air.
The dust moves, but the air is still.*
And I really like that because we often sit in our kitchen where the sun is coming in and see all these little bubbles that we usually don't see.
Anyway, I like that analogy.
*So thus, by consideration of this example, the dust, which as it moves obscures the air, and the air, which itself remains still, I understand that the dust may signify motion.
The Buddha said, "So it is."*
So the commentary, hi Toy.
The commentary:

*When the sun has just come up early on a clear fresh morning after the rain, the sun shines through a crack in the door or perhaps a crack in the wall, and it displays fine bits of dust bobbing up and down in space, moving all around in the sunshine.
If the sun doesn't shine in the doorway, you can't see the dust, although there is actually a lot of dust everywhere.
But while the dust moves, bobbing up and down, the space is still, it doesn't move.
The ability to see the dust in the light that pours through the crack represents the attainment of the light of wisdom.
When you reach the first stage of an arhat and overcome the 88 kinds of diluted awareness, you have that light of wisdom.
Then you can see your ignorance, which moves like the dust in the sunlight and which causes many afflictions out there, as many as the sand grains in the River Ganges.
You will also see the unmoving stillness of your essential nature.*
So I really liked that analogy and it reminded me of a song that we used to sing.
I'm going to sing just a little teeny song, Chris, from Palm Village, where everybody would sing in a group and take turns filling in, substituting the word cloud.
So I'll talk about that.
But this little song goes:
*My mind is a clear blue sky.
My mind is a clear blue sky.
Clouds come and clouds go.
My mind is a clear blue sky.*
And so then people would shout out thoughts, dust, pain, worries, joys, whatever, and we would sing it in that song.
That song feels to me like this analogy with the dust in the space.
So in a couple more pages, the commentary continues:
*You must recognize the pure luminous essential nature of the everlasting true mind and your mad distinction-making mind must cease.*
By the way, hi Kim and Eric and Toy.
I'm not sure who was here when, but we are on part two, the nature of visual awareness.
And there are several chapters in here.
It's the mind that sees; visual awareness does not move.
That's the place that I'm on right now.
So in the commentary, he says again:
*It is said the ceasing of the mad mind is full awakening.*
This again reminds me of Ty's definition of nirvana, which is the extinction of ideas and notions.
*The mad mind's coming to a stop is the manifestation of our awakened mind.
Because the mad mind exists and has not ceased, the awakened mind cannot come forth.
The mad mind covers it over,*
kind of like the clouds in the blue sky.
*The aim of this passage*
—I thought this was a good line—
*The aim of this passage and every passage of the Shurangama Sutra, without exception, is to reveal one's true mind.*
So in chapter three, called Visual Awareness Does Not Perish, this chapter begins with a statement from King Prazanajit.
Prazanajit.
*Before I was instructed by the Buddha, I met two persons, contemporaries of the Buddha, who taught forms of skepticism.
They said that this body dies and when it dies, we cease to exist and become nothing.
That very nothingness is called nirvana.*
The king stated that even though he had now met the Buddha, he still had doubts that made him curious.
So this chapter alludes to the fact that the everlasting mind does not perish in the same way that things of form do.
The Buddha says:
*I now will reveal to you what it is that does not come into being and what does not perish.
Your majesty, your face is wrinkled.
What does not wrinkle does not change.
What changes will perish.
But what does not change neither comes into being nor perishes.
Then how could it be affected by your being born or dying?
So you have no need to be concerned with what such people say, that when this body dies, you cease to exist.*
The king believed the words that he had said, and he understood that when we leave this body, we go on to another.
So I have a little comment here because it raised a little bit of a red flag for me.
This is just totally my opinion.
I read that and for me, I see that the everlasting true mind is something that exists in all things.
But I don't have ownership of that true mind in me.
It's true mind in all things.

So in my mind, I don't see that we as individuals continue as an intact form, that all of the interconnected elements that made up this manifestation of me, of this particular form, do not cease to exist and do merely continue manifesting in various forms as conditions are present.
Anyway, that's my take.
So in our breakout session tonight, that can be one of the topics if you feel like you want to talk about that a little.
Chapter four is called The Nature of Visual Awareness Is Not Lost.
In this chapter, the Buddha says:

*All good people, I have often said that all phenomena with physical form, all phenomena of mind, the conditions under which they arise as well as the phenomena that interact with the mind, and all conditioned phenomena are mere manifestations of the true mind, of true mind.
Your bodies and minds appear within the wondrous light of the true essence of that wondrous mind.
What you do not know is that true wondrous luminously understanding mind contains the body and everything outside the body, mountains, rivers, sky, the entire world.
You are someone who fails to see a boundless ocean 100,000 miles across and is aware only of a single floating bubble.
You see that bubble floating and think it is the vast tide that surges toward the farthest branches of the sea.*
So here's another commentary.
Every time I say it's a commentary, unless I say me, it's by Master Xuan Hua.
So he says:
*Most people think the mind is within the body.
That is a great mistake.
It is neither inside nor outside.
It is not that our minds are within our bodies, but that we are within the true mind.
Our mind encompasses empty space and the 10,000 things.
It is not that empty space and 10,000 things contain us.
If you understand this doctrine, you have not lost track of your true mind.*
So I'll repeat this at the end because this is another little piece that you may want to talk about in the breakout group.
But I'll remind you, I'll repeat it.
Chapter five is visual awareness is not dependent on conditions.
So I'm going to read just this little part of the chapter.
It says:
*What makes distinctions about visual objects and all objects cannot do so independently of the visual objects it distinguishes.*
Does that make sense?
So everything in our mind when we're having an opinion, when we're labeling it, whatever, we hear the bird song, that it doesn't exist without the object.
If there wasn't any bird song, I wouldn't hear the bird song.
So he's just saying that the part of us that makes distinctions cannot do that independently.
There has to be an object that it distinguishes.
So your mind that makes distinctions does not exist independently of the objects that it distinguishes.

*And when the making of distinctions ceases, such that neither space nor objects are distinguished, even then, your mind does not have a distinction-making nature that exists independent of objects of mind.
Thus, each of your mental states is dependent on something, something else.*
They are not like the innkeeper at the end.
So chapter six was called visual awareness is not a perceived object.
In this chapter, all I did is include the commentary.
It says:
*The Buddha told Ananda that visual awareness is not an object, but Ananda doesn't believe him yet.
So the Buddha has to make it clear for him.
If visual awareness were an object, then visual awareness would be visible.
Therefore, Ananda should be able to see the Buddha's visual awareness, because if visual awareness were an object, it would have attributes which could be distinguished.
In fact, however, visual awareness has no form or appearance.
It is neither green, yellow, red, white or black, neither long or short, square, round.
It isn't a thing.
And so you can't see it.
If you can say, "Oh, basically, my visual awareness does not come and does not go," basically does not come into being and does not perish.
If you understand this doctrine, then you'll understand the nature of visual awareness.*
So here's a little comment in here.
Gosh, the time goes fast.
I need to hurry.
My comment was, I can think of a lot of things that are not visible and still objects of the senses.
So here's one that I thought gives me a little blip in the logic here.
What about sounds or tastes or thoughts?
We can't see those either.
But they are still objects within the conditioned world.
So anyway, chapter seven.
This is pretty quick because I want to leave room for breakouts.
Visual awareness has neither shape nor extension.
The Buddha said, "Do not say that your awareness itself expands or contracts."
He gives examples of air contained in different shaped containers.
And when these are removed, the shape has neither shape.
Has neither shape [unclear: "of I think I miss them"].
Like if you had space in a square box and space in a round box, when you remove those boxes, the shape wouldn't stay like square or round.
*From the time without beginning, all beings have mistakenly identified themselves with what they are aware of, controlled by their experience of perceived objects.
They lose track of their fundamental minds.
In this state, they perceive visual awareness as large or small.
But when they are in control of their experience, they see they are the same as the Thus Come Ones.*
I'm going to go on to chapter eight.
Visual awareness is both separate and not separate from objects.
The Buddha conversed with Ananda and said, "Your visual awareness does not have a nature of its own that is distinct from the myriad things.
Thus, your awareness is not something you can point out."
Ananda said, "I do not think that anything I see as I look around the Grove is separate from my awareness."

**IkuShun Desiree Webster:** *Why?
If the trees were separate from my awareness, how could I be seeing them?
If the trees were identical to my awareness, how could they still be trees?
The same is true of every perceived object and of space as well.
If space were separate from my awareness, how could I be seeing it?
But if it were identical to my awareness, how could it still be space?
Having re-examined this, having considered in detail the myriad sites around us, I realized that not even the smallest of them is separate from my awareness.
The Buddha said, so it is, so it is.*
This brings to mind for me the Heart Sutra.
Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.
In the commentary: *there is no is or is not.

Space and objects like our awareness are the true mind.* Later, it's explained that the four primary elements, earth, fire, wind, and water, are the matrix of the Thus Come One, which Chris is going to talk about here in a second.
Identity and separation are relative concepts, but what is spoken of here is the absolute.
So quickly, in Chapter 9, visual awareness arises neither on its own nor from causes.
And Chapter 10, true visual awareness: both of those, for me, are a continuation of the phrase from the Heart Sutra.
Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.
You can explore these chapters a little bit more.
There are a couple paragraphs from each chapter.
In Chapter 9, it says:

*Therefore, you should understand the existence of an essential wondrously understanding enlightened visual awareness is not dependent for its existence on causes and conditions, nor does it exist in and of itself.
Nor can one say that it is independent of causes and conditions.*
Did I skip something?
*Nor does it exist in and of itself.
Nor can one say that it is independent of causes and conditions.
Statements that account for its existence cannot be negated, yet one cannot say that they cannot be negated.
Such statements cannot be affirmed, yet one cannot say that they cannot be affirmed.*
These are like tetralemmas.
The first paragraph of the last commentary at the end of Chapter 10 again reminds me not only of the half, form is emptiness, but of not forgetting the other half of this, which is emptiness is form.
*True reality is true emptiness and it is also wondrous existence.
Do you say that true emptiness is empty?
It is not because within it all that exists comes into being.
True emptiness is said to be true because it is not in fact empty, and all that exists is wondrous because it does not in fact exist.
What exists within emptiness is wondrous existence.*
I won't keep going on, but it's just this whole thing: I have an easy time thinking that form is emptiness, but I have a harder time remembering that emptiness is form.
I really liked these whole chapters in this part, because they really speak about the connection.
You can't just say form is emptiness without saying emptiness is form.
They go together.
In Chapter 11, he just talks about distortions in everyone's perceptions due to their own karma, both their individual karma and their collective karma.
Everyone has individual aspects about them because of both of these kinds of karma.
And lastly, visual awareness exists neither through inhering nor in conjoining.
This is a little difficult.
I'll just summarize here by saying that the Buddha is describing a tetralemma.
The enlightened nature of visual awareness does not arise from causes and conditions, and it does not come into being on its own.

But it also does not exist because of [unclear: "in hearing"], which is inseparable [unclear: "in hearing"] of essential qualities, or because of conjoining, which is the coming together of two substances in ways that do not change their distinct essential natures, nor because of a lack of [unclear: "in hearing"] and a lack of conjoining.
So again, it's like a tetralemma at the end: it's not this, it's not that, it's not both, and it's not neither.
That's the end of what I have for part two.
Now I would like everybody to get into breakout groups.

You can talk about anything that stood out for you in my fast talk, or you can talk about that quote I read from the commentary that said that most people think that the mind is within the body, but really all things are within the mind.
So you can talk about that.
Sorry, do you want to put it into the chat feature so people can take it with them when they go off into the breakout rooms?
It's hard for me to type that whole thing in there.

The easiest thing is to just talk about something that stands out, or agreement or whatever, in what I talked about last time or this time. 12345678, so maybe you can put some people in a group of three and then two people are going to be in a group of two.
How about all groups of two.
Okay, breakout rooms.
Well, two groups are three, and then one group is two.
How about I stick you in a breakout room too?
That's fine, whatever is easier.
Because I know we have like three minutes each or something before we come back.
Please self time.
Yeah.
You all found your way back.
I confess my favorite paragraph in the chapter on visual awareness comes from Manjushri.
*Then Manjushri, Prince of Dharma, taking pity on the four assemblies, stood up amidst the gathering.

Having bowed at the Buddha's feet, he put his palms together in respect and said to the Buddha, World Honored One, the Great Assembly has not understood the two disclosures that the Thus Come One has made.
First, that the essence of our visual awareness and visible objects and space as well are identical.
And second, that they're not identical.*
All right.
So, the next chapter is the matrix of the Thus Come One.
Chris, sorry, do we want, is there time for a break or should we just keep going?
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Let's have a five minute break.
Okay.
Can someone remind me after the break to turn the recording back on?
Okay.
All right.
Thanks.
Five minutes.
What I'm going to read first is the summary that's in the beginning of the book.
Roman 20 is if you're looking for the page.
It's not that much, so I'm just going to read this.
*Part three, the matrix of the Thus Come One.
The question remains, why would we want to stop paying attention to the conditioned world?
The answer is twofold.
First, our involvement in that world is fraught with dissatisfaction and suffering.
And second, that the world, as we see it, is not real.
It is the second point that the Buddha now turns to.

He begins by declaring, Fundamentally, everything that comes and goes, that comes into being and ceases to be, is within the true nature of the matrix of the Thus Come One, which is the wondrous, everlasting understanding, the unmoving, all-pervading, wondrous suchness of reality.*
So, yeah, the matrix of the Thus Come One, we could call it Tathagata, Garba, the womb of all Buddhas, true nature, true mind, Buddha nature, Buddha mind, it all covers the same.
*But then the Buddha continues by demonstrating the truth of this position.
Each of the elements of the physical world and each of our senses is not showing us true reality.
Everything is filtered and conditioned.*
So that's the summary of the nature of the Thus Come One.
Now I'm stopping to quote from the good book here.
I hope that you all had the opportunity to practice with the Shurangama Sutra a little last week.
I sent out that koan with commentaries.
And how else can we practice with the Shurangama?
Like all Buddhist teachings, it is not about something external.
It's not something we study in detail so we can compartmentalize it.
But we should take what we learn from the Shurangama and integrate it as something to recognize within our own experience.
The question is, how can we find out what is true for ourselves?
Dogen says in Genjokoan:
*When you sail out in a boat to the middle of the ocean where no land is in sight and view the four directions, the ocean looks circular and does not look any other way.
But the ocean is neither round nor square.
Its features are infinite in variety.
It is like a palace.
It is like a jewel.
It only looks circular as far as you can see at the time.
All things are like this.
Though there are many features in the dusty world and the world beyond conditions, you see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach.*
End quote.
With this quote in mind, please understand that Desiree and I don't teach you anything new here.
But the hope is to give the eye of practice a little bit more play, another perspective.
So how do we practice the Shurangama with that in mind?
Zazen, silent illumination.
[unclear: "Justice"]. [unclear: "Justice"] is taking our place between heaven and earth. [unclear: "Justice"].
And we are taking our place in Buddha's mind, in Buddha nature.

In the midst of the daily grind of washing the dishes and arguing with the internet provider on the phone, bawling our eyes out because we are feeling grief, the grief of the entire world, and yet we do all this surrounded by Buddha nature and Buddha mind.
And when we find something to be unbearable, when something is beyond our capacity to tolerate, we bear witness.
We see and we remember.
We do what we can.
And yet when the time comes, we take our seat, and we take our seat bearing our own Buddha nature in the middle of Buddha's mind.

As Desiree demonstrated today, and we talked a little about it last week, according to the Shurangama Sutra, the location of the mind is not limited to a specific physical location, and how it is repeated so many times: it is not inside us, nor outside, nor in between.
Instead, the Sutra teaches that the mind is inherently luminous and expansive and that true nature, our true nature, all true nature, transcends conventional notions of location and boundary.
So Buddha mind is a dynamic and interconnected aspect of consciousness and it pervades all phenomena.
It is not confined to the physical body, but encompasses the entirety of existence, of the universe.
The mind is described as boundless and immeasurable, and the true nature goes beyond conceptualization and limitation.
The mind is depicted as the source of all experiences and perceptions and at the same time constantly interacting with the world, and the mind is shaping our reality through its activities.
However, all functions that bring the world forward are illuminated by true nature.
It is the mirror that reflects whatever it perceives.
But then I might ask, why do I continue to struggle so much?
Why am I wrestling with this bear for the hundredth time?
One answer is that I am human, and my conditioned mind, my ego, wants to create a world in which it thinks me safe.
So it creates a small, limited world.
But I say this small world is illusory too.
Because, this is really important, it's illusory because there is no small life.
That life we have, specifically yours, it is not a small life.
Let me say it a third time.
There is no small life.
Another thing that keeps on coming up is mindfulness.
Has anybody here taken any mindfulness classes, mindfulness courses?
Anybody?
Ah, majority here.
In the context of Buddhism and the Shurangama Sutra, mindfulness is a wonderful thing, I like it.
I did become an instructor.
But there is one tiny little problem with mindfulness.
Does anybody have an idea what that might be?
You're always mindful of something.
That means in order to practice mindfulness, we have an object we are mindful of.
If you're mindfully washing dishes or mindfully taking a shower, it's all that kind of sensory input.
And Desiree has just told us it's not quite as real as we think it is.
But true mind cannot be the object of your mindfulness.
Whatever we are mindful of is a concept, it's an object, and true mind falls outside of those categories.
I'm so sorry.
I just want to really make clear that mindfulness is a wonderful thing, but it doesn't quite fit the bill in this context.
We are trying to reach beyond, to go beyond the conceptual that we can think our way through.
I know I touched on the mind only school last time, and the Shurangama Sutra comes closer to the mind only school than to mindfulness.
In the mind only school, phenomena are understood to arise from the mind itself.
It basically challenges the notion of an external objective reality, independent of consciousness, with phenomena seen as projections or manifestations of the mind.
We talked about the consciousnesses last time.
I just want to bring up the three natures, because that plays somewhat into what we're talking about today.
In the mind only school, basically phenomena have three natures.
One is the dependent nature, one is the imaginary nature, and the other one is the perfected nature.
Having these categories helps in that system to explain the nature of phenomena.
*[Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster share this talk.
Speaker labels mark the handovers the recording makes clear.
In some stretches the recording does not show which of them is speaking, so those passages carry no new label.]*
What the mind only school shares with the Shurangama is that it really investigates the nature of consciousness and the nature of mind.
So now I wanted to read the opening of chapter 3 of the Matrix of the Daskhaman.
I just want to repeat for more time that in this context you could use the mother of all Buddhas, the womb of all Buddhas, true nature, true mind, mind only.
You can throw it all together as a workable field of exploration for this.
And let's remember again that in the last session the Buddha sent Manjushri out to yank Ananda out of the bed of a very beautiful courtesan.
And they are now in front of the Buddha, and Ananda, the fall guy, the Buddha has to explain things to him slowly in small words.
*Ananda, you have not yet understood that the objects we perceive are unreal and illusory.
They are subject to change, appearing here and there and disappearing here and there.
Yet these illusions, each with its conventional designation, are in fact within the essential wondrous enlightenment.
The same is true of the five aggregates, the six faculties, the twelve sides and the eighteen constituent elements.
It is an illusion that they come into being when both their causes and their conditions are present.
And it is an illusion that they cease when either their causes or their conditions are absent.

You simply have not yet understood that fundamentally everything that comes and goes, that comes into being and ceases to be, is within the true matrix of the Das Kamman, which is the wondrous, everlasting understanding, the unmoving, all-pervading wondrous suchness of reality.*
Wait a minute, doesn't that go against all our Buddhist teaching?

The Buddha just said that the five skandhas and mind, the six faculties, hearing, seeing, etc. and the twelve sides, which is a combination of eye and visible object, ear and sound, and the eighteen constituent elements, which is a mind that receives the input from the eyes of an object that is seen.
Does that make sense to everybody?
I'm not understanding why you feel that that last sentence is against or opposite of...
Because we always say in true mind, that true mind supersedes our regular reality, that everything is impermanent, that nothing has an inherent self.

And here Buddha says that everything that arises and ceases, so all phenomena, all our senses, all our emotions, everything, is within the true nature of the matrix of the Das Kamman, so that means that everything is impermanent.
We don't see it as permanent, but something that arises out of the Buddha nature.
That's what the sutra posits.

So instead of seeing things as just rising and falling away, not so worthy of our attention and engagement, in this sutra it says that all these things that come and go, they do not come and go independently, they come and go within the framework of Buddha nature and Buddha mind.
That seems to go with what I think, though, in terms of everything is within true nature, everything.
That's why you're always five steps ahead of me.
No, I'm just wondering.
It didn't feel like a contradiction to me.
Well, it shifts the perspective a little bit, you know, the way I usually see things.

So the Buddha continues, that though you may seek within the everlasting reality of the matrix of the Das Kamman for what comes and goes, for confusion and awakening, and for coming into being and ceasing to be, you will not find it there.
And then the commentary by Xuan Hua is really good on this section.
When you do not understand there is coming and going, there is confusion and enlightenment, there is birth, death and rebirth.

But if you understand the everlasting true mind, if you recognize your own fundamental nature, the pure nature and luminous essence of the everlasting true mind, you put an end to all the illusory coming into being and ceasing to be.
So that is his commentary on this section.
So in the matrix of the Das Kamman, the third chapter here in this book, the Buddha lists basically all the elements of the world.
He lists the five aggregates: the aggregate of form, sense, perception, cognition, mental formations.
And then he adds the aggregate of consciousness.
Out of those arise the six faculties, which is the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and so on.
And then this is a repeat of what I just said.
The 12 sides are the faculty in combination with the object.
So eyes, invisible objects, ear faculty and sounds, nose faculty and odors, and so on.
The 18 constituents, sometimes you hear them also called 18 datus, are the coming into being of eye consciousness in combination with the eye and the visible object.
Ear consciousness in combination with ear and audible sound.
Nose consciousness in combination with nose and a smell that you can detect, and so on.
And last but not least, the sutra lists seven primary elements.
We usually know earth, fire, water and wind as the four primary elements.
And in this sutra, they added three more: the primary elements of space, of awareness and consciousness.
So let me just go back to my written notes.
